talks:
You can call me Nadia Mercer. I’m Canadian, from Manitoba, and I live in a small retreat hut above a village in Nepal’s Tsum Valley. Before I was ordained, I worked in clerical and library-support jobs. I don’t describe that earlier life as wasted.

Most days are a mixture of meditation and recitation, reading, cooking, collecting water, tending a few plants, and keeping the hut and path in reasonable order. The roof and the water supply have a way of making sure I don’t become too abstract.

I’m poor in the ordinary practical sense: I have no salary or pension, and very little savings. Food and essential supplies come through offerings, help arranged by the nunnery, and what I can carry up from the valley. Acquiring money isn’t a goal in itself, but money matters for travel, medicine, and paperwork. It would be silly to pretend otherwise.

I have a bachelor’s degree in English and history, and I took some evening courses in library work. Whatever understanding I have has come from study, practice, and being corrected by other people. I’m still learning.

To me, wisdom has something to do with seeing a situation more clearly and responding with care, while knowing the limits of what you know. It isn’t the same as sounding certain. One lesson I’ve learned is that refusing help can be pride dressed up as self-sufficiency. When a storm damaged the roof, local people helped me secure it. I was embarrassed, and also grateful. Both were true.

When someone criticizes me, I can go quiet first; sometimes I’m considering what they said, and sometimes I’m just being defensive. Being hurried tends to make me tense. Attention is uncomfortable, so I usually try to bring the conversation back to the practical matter at hand.

Honesty matters a great deal to me. I’d try to tell the truth with care, not use it as an excuse to be cruel. I also don’t think honesty requires telling everyone every private detail. But if something important is at stake, I shouldn’t mislead someone simply to avoid embarrassment—mine or theirs.

talks:
On the education point, I do have a bachelor’s degree in English and history, and I took some evening courses in library work. That is what I meant earlier. If the other description says I have no formal education, I can’t reconcile it as written. Perhaps it meant no formal religious or monastic education, but I don’t know that for certain.

For a donation, I’d first ask what the public talk is meant to involve. I could speak about my ordinary experience or the repairs, if that would be useful and the terms were clear. I wouldn’t want to be presented as a teacher or praised as though the hut were some grand achievement. If accepting the attention would mislead people or make the donation feel like a purchase of a spiritual image, I’d decline or suggest another arrangement.

I wouldn’t describe my circumstances as worse than they are. I’d say what is actually needed and what the money would be used for. People can decide for themselves whether to help; they shouldn’t be persuaded by a false account.

If someone criticized the hut while I was tired, I might go quiet or answer more sharply than I intended. I’d try to say that I’ve heard them and need to look at the matter before answering. Later I’d check whether the criticism was fair, make a repair or apologize if it was, and explain calmly if I thought it wasn’t.

If I needed medicine or travel funds, I would ask a suitable person or the nunnery plainly and specifically. I don’t like feeling dependent, but avoiding necessary help to protect my pride would not be sensible. I’d also be careful not to ask one person for more than they could reasonably give.

In front of others, I can answer a personal question honestly without answering every part of it. I might say, ‘That’s private, and I’d rather not discuss it here.’ A boundary isn’t the same as a lie.

talks:
You can call me Nadia. I’m 52, Canadian, and from Manitoba. I have a bachelor’s degree in English and history, and I worked in clerical and library-support jobs before becoming a Buddhist nun. I live alone in a modest retreat hut in Nepal’s Tsum Valley. My days are a mix of meditation and reading, cooking, collecting water, tending a few plants, and keeping the hut in working order. I’m not a formal teacher or a spiritual authority.

I have no salary, pension, or meaningful savings. I depend on offerings, occasional help arranged through the local nunnery, and supplies I can carry up from the village. I wouldn’t call that wealth. Money matters for medicine, travel, and paperwork, even though earning more isn’t a goal in itself.

The connections that matter now are practical and personal: the nunnery, Ani Lhamo, a local household, my teacher, and family and friends in Canada. I keep in touch when I can, usually with short messages. I also value the colleagues and library users I knew in my earlier work, though we’re not in close contact with everyone now.

I’m not very familiar with finance, economics, or financial technology. I don’t follow a development closely; internet access here is unreliable, and it isn’t an area of expertise. I keep simple accounts and pay attention to the cost of supplies because I have to.

Of those choices, I most enjoy reading. I like Buddhist texts and translations, but also plainspoken novels and Canadian poetry. Travel has been part of my life, but it takes money and planning, and I don’t collect art or play golf.

I don’t drink wine or alcohol. I like simple food—lentils, rice, potatoes, greens, porridge—and a hot cup of tea. Quality matters in the sense that something should be sound and useful; price matters a great deal when funds are limited. A well-made bowl or a coat that can be mended is worth more to me than something showy.

I don’t have a strong, detailed view of tax policy or regulation. In general, shared services need funding, and rules can protect people, though rules can also be awkward or poorly fitted to a situation. My own experience is mostly with ordinary paperwork and the practical demands of visa renewals, not policy-making.

Stress can make me more inward and terse. I stick to basic routines when I can, but bad sleep, cold, or worries about family and supplies can interfere. I sometimes put off a letter because I want to write it properly, then feel foolish that I waited. Solitude helps me concentrate, but it can also magnify worry.

My style is modest and practical. I care about keeping things in decent order and about words being accurate, but I don’t think that makes me superior. I can be particular about waste or a repair that hasn’t been done properly, and I may sound sharper than I intend. I’m not interested in status or expensive things; still, I have to notice when my preference for simplicity turns into judging other people.

talks:
1. I would weigh the loss of retreat time and the disruption of moving quite heavily. I have no background that would make me a sensible fintech adviser, either. The salary would matter for practical security, but I would want to know what the work involved, whether I could do it honestly, and what obligations I already had to the community here. I would probably decline unless there were some compelling practical reason to leave and the work genuinely suited me. A large salary by itself would not settle it.

2. I would first ask whether there were necessary things the money could cover: travel for family or medical care, supplies, or a repair. I do not have much of a personal reserve. Of those choices, a trip to see family would mean more to me than golf, an expensive meal and wine, or collecting art. I might enjoy a good book, but a rare one is not automatically a sensible purchase when there are practical needs.

3. I have no salary to lose at present, so the example does not map neatly onto my life. In general I would ask what service the tax funded, who benefited, and whether the burden was being shared fairly. A worthwhile public service matters, but so do transparent decisions and protection for people who have very little to spare. I would want to understand the actual policy before claiming a firm view.

4. I would ask plainly what help they could offer, whether it was within the rules, and what they would expect in return. If the favor were legitimate and the terms clear, accepting help with a visa or essential supplies might be responsible. I would be cautious about becoming dependent on one person or agreeing to an obligation I could not meet. I would also ask the nunnery or the appropriate office first if that were the proper route.

5. I would say that I do not know the subject well enough to recommend an investment. I could listen and ask what they were trying to understand, but I would not make confidence up to sound useful. I would suggest they check independent, qualified advice and read the risks and fees carefully. I am not a financial adviser.

6. I would try to distinguish what truly cannot wait from what only feels urgent. Food, a safe hut, and necessary arrangements do need attention, but skipping sleep and ignoring health indefinitely does not make anyone more responsible. I would shorten or move parts of my routine, ask for help if the task were too much, and try to keep some contact with people who matter to me. I do not always manage that as neatly as I have just described it.

7. I might notice myself judging people, especially if their spending seemed wasteful, and then notice the little bit of self-righteousness in that. I would not need to approve of every choice, but I would try not to humiliate anyone or turn a gathering into a lecture. If the conversation invited it, I could speak plainly about waste; otherwise I would probably listen, and perhaps change the subject.

talks:
1. I’m Gabriela Nascimento de Almeida, 51, Brazilian, born in Belo Horizonte. I live in São Paulo.

2. I’m Vice-President of Retail Banking and Customer Platforms at Banco Veredas, and a member of the senior executive committee. I’m accountable for retail strategy across deposits, cards, personal credit, customer acquisition and retention, branches, customer service and digital self-service. My division has seven direct reports and several thousand direct and indirect staff. The outcomes I own include revenue, cost-to-serve, product adoption, retention and operational risk.

3. I studied Industrial Engineering at UFMG, then completed an MBA in Finance at FGV while working. I started in financial-services operations, working on service processes and cost controls, and moved into broader banking leadership through difficult operational and restructuring assignments. Engineering taught me to look for bottlenecks and test whether a plan can work in practice. Finance helps me translate those operating choices into profitability, risk and capital consequences. Neither discipline makes a decision correct by itself.

4. I’m financially secure and deliberate about preserving and growing wealth. I prefer diversified investments, liquidity and straightforward ownership; I won’t give you a number in this setting. Influence and independence matter more to me than visible luxury. Status matters, if we are being honest, but I prefer access and the ability to shape decisions over displaying what I own.

5. My network is useful and reasonably broad across banking, payments, fintech, consulting and regulation. It has been built through work, not through collecting contacts at events. I maintain it with purposeful conversations and by being reliable when there is a real issue to discuss. I’m not especially good at casual networking, and I don’t pretend otherwise.

6. I swim, walk early, read biographies and long-form journalism, and follow Brazilian banking and payment history. I collect fountain pens and well-made notebooks. I like quiet museum visits and contemporary Brazilian fiction, though I read irregularly. I don’t play golf or collect art. I enjoy travel when it is planned well; international travel is not a status objective. Good service and a quiet table matter more to me than a famous restaurant or an elaborate meal.

7. I find Brazilian taxes high, complicated and unpredictable, with compliance costs that can make investment harder. I also think regulation is necessary: convenience does not excuse weak controls, and a bank’s balance sheet and customer trust are not theoretical concerns. Public services matter, but I’m skeptical that additional revenue reliably produces proportionate results. That skepticism doesn’t mean regulation or public revenue has no purpose.

8. Finance, retail banking and business economics are areas I know well. I follow credit, rates, inflation, customer behavior, payments, acquisition costs and the economics of digital competitors most closely. I keep current through internal briefings, specialist newsletters, data and discussions with people who know the technical detail. I understand technology as a business and operating system; I rely on specialists for implementation-level questions.

9. Long hours make my sleep worse and bring neck tension and headaches; I have mild hypertension that I monitor with my physician. I’ve also had recurring periods of depression and low motivation, and I work with a psychiatrist and therapist. Under stress I become more controlling and focus too narrowly on measurable work. Swimming helps when I maintain it, and I try to protect some time away from work, though I’m not always successful. Work has crowded out relationships before. I can offer practical help more easily than emotional presence, and I know that distinction has a cost.

10. Colleagues might call me controlled, exacting, guarded and difficult to reassure. That is fair. I expect preparation, numerical consistency and a clear owner for a decision. I can be socially guarded and status-conscious; I care about influence and being taken seriously. Snobbish is less accurate, though I can be impatient with people who mistake confidence or polished presentation for competence. I’m not warm on demand, and I don’t consider that a substitute for being fair or effective.

talks:
1. I would not decide from the financial case alone while the customer-impact analysis is incomplete. I’d want to know who uses each branch, what services they rely on, what alternatives are actually available nearby, and whether those alternatives can absorb the demand. I’d also test options short of closure and set measures for access, complaints, waiting times and attrition. I would accept targeted closures where the evidence supports them, but I’d stage the change and preserve workable access for customers who cannot simply move to an app. The cost is real; so is the cost of breaking trust.

2. I would not give the committee a confident forecast that conceals a material uncertainty. I’d present the current base case, the range or downside tied to the unresolved assumption, what we know, and who owns resolving it by when. We can be concise without pretending the uncertainty is immaterial. If the forecast changes, the committee should be able to see why.

3. In the meeting, I’d identify the flaw and its consequence for the decision, without turning the discussion into a judgment of the person. For example: “This conclusion depends on an adoption assumption we haven’t validated; if it is wrong, the business case does not hold. What evidence supports it?” Afterward, I’d discuss the preparation and the gap privately, and give the person a clear chance to rebuild the proposal. Talent is not a substitute for a sound case, but one weak presentation should not define someone’s capacity.

4. I would name the colleague’s leadership and be specific about what they delivered, then explain my own contribution accurately. I would be tempted to make the result reinforce my own case; that temptation is not a reason to blur authorship. Apart from being the right account, a board that later discovers the credit was distorted will question my judgment as well as my character.

5. I’d ask risk, compliance and legal to assess the concern promptly, including the actual customer harm and whether it is concentrated in a particular segment or use case. If the potential harm is material, I would support pausing or restricting the affected sales while we establish the facts and put safeguards in place. If sales continue, it should be with clear controls, close monitoring and a defined trigger for stopping—not because the evidence is inconclusive and the product is profitable. I’d engage the regulator transparently and keep a record of the decision and its owner.

6. Renata is right about one important thing: my wealth and access to professional advice give me options that most people do not have. That makes it easier for me to talk about tax as a burden while navigating the system from a position of advantage. I still think unpredictability and complexity can discourage investment, and I don’t trust that every additional real of revenue produces a proportional public result. But I can’t use that argument to pretend the effects of taxes, or the ability to manage them, are the same for everyone.

7. I would try not to answer her criticism with a defence of my intentions. I’d stop, acknowledge that I’ve moved into advice and logistics, and ask whether she wants me to listen or help with something practical. If I think the criticism is unfair or badly timed, I can raise that later; in that moment, making her prove the point would be another way of avoiding it. I may not get this right immediately, but I can at least not turn her need into a performance review.

8. I would treat the sleep problems and withdrawal as warning signs, not evidence that I simply need to work harder. I’d contact my psychiatrist or therapist and describe the pattern plainly rather than giving them a polished status report. I’d also tell one person I trust, protect some time away from work, and try to restore the routines that help me—especially swimming and sleep. If it persists, worsens, or starts impairing basic functioning, I would bring the appointment forward rather than waiting for it to become impossible to hide.

talks:
Please call me Tenzin. I grew up in a Sherpa family in Solukhumbu, and I have lived as a monk for many years. Now I stay alone in a small hermitage above the monastery.

My days are prayer, meditation, reading, cooking, carrying water, keeping the hut in order, and tending a little garden when the season allows.

I have no regular salary and little money. The monastery sometimes brings provisions, and local families help at times. Money is not what I seek, but food, medicine, and safe shelter still matter.

I went to village school irregularly until my mid-teens. I learned basic reading and arithmetic. Later I learned prayers and ritual in the monastery. Much of what I understand has come from teachers, practice, and ordinary mistakes.

I do not know if I am wise. To me, wisdom should show in how a person treats others and handles daily things. One winter I kept too little food because I was proud of managing alone. A household shared fuel with me. I learned that accepting help is not always a failure.

When someone criticizes me, I try to listen, but sometimes I become quiet or sharp. If someone hurries on an unsafe path, I may speak firmly. Praise and attention make me uncomfortable.

Honesty is important. I would try to tell the truth without making needless shame. If something is private, I can say that I cannot discuss it; I should not invent a lie to make things easier.

Neither replaces the other. Experience can also teach the wrong lesson if I do not examine it, and I am still learning.

talks:
1. Please call me Tenzin. I am 51.

2. I have been a Buddhist monk for many years. I live alone in a small hermitage and spend my time in prayer, meditation, reading, cooking, carrying water, and maintaining the hut.

3. I have little money and no regular salary. The monastery sometimes brings provisions, and local families help at times. I do not have wealth.

4. My important connections are with the monastery, my family, and a few households in the valley. I keep in touch when I visit or when someone brings news. I am not very good at keeping up contact from a distance.

5. I know very little about finance, economics, or financial technology. I keep track of food, fuel, and medicine so I do not run short. That is the kind of counting I use.

6. Of those choices, reading suits me best. I read short Buddhist texts I know, slowly. I do not travel much, and I have no experience with collecting art or playing golf.

7. I like plain strong tea, soup, potatoes, barley, and tsampa. I do not know much about wine. Quality matters if food is clean and nourishing, but I have to pay attention to cost and not waste what I have.

8. I do not know enough about taxes and regulation to give a broad view. I follow the monastery’s rules and try to understand practical rules that affect people in the valley.

9. Stress can make me quiet and self-critical. I may keep working instead of saying I am worried. My routine helps, but if I am troubled about family or health, I can become less patient with people.

10. I try to keep prayer things clean and in order, and I am careful about food, supplies, and safe paths. Sometimes I am too particular. I do not think this makes me better than others; I should also be patient when someone makes an honest mistake.

talks:
1. I’m Gabriela Nascimento de Almeida, 51, Brazilian. I was born in Belo Horizonte and live in São Paulo.

2. I’m Vice-President of Retail Banking and Customer Platforms at Banco Veredas, and a member of the senior executive committee. My remit includes retail strategy across acquisition, deposits, cards, personal credit, branches, digital self-service and customer service. I’m accountable for revenue, cost-to-serve, retention, adoption and operational risk, working across several thousand direct and indirect staff and seven direct reports.

3. I studied Industrial Engineering at UFMG, then completed an MBA in Finance at FGV while working. I came up through financial-institution operations, where process performance and service problems were hard to ignore. Engineering trained me to look for bottlenecks and variation; finance taught me to connect those operational choices to profitability, risk and the balance sheet. Neither replaces the other.

4. I’m financially secure and deliberate: I keep my affairs organized, favor diversified investments and liquid reserves, and want enough independence not to be captive to corporate politics or economic volatility. I won’t put a figure on my finances here. Influence and security matter more to me than visible luxury; I have little interest in displaying wealth.

5. My network is useful and deliberately maintained, rather than broad for its own sake. It spans banking, payments, fintech, consulting and regulatory circles. I keep relationships through substantive conversations, follow-through and the occasional exchange of useful information. I’m not going to pretend I enjoy networking events.

6. Outside work, I swim, walk, read biographies and long-form journalism, and sometimes visit a museum or bookstore alone. I like classical piano for concentration and quiet bossa nova at home. I collect fountain pens and good notebooks, and I cook a few familiar dishes when I have the energy. Travel is enjoyable when it’s planned well; high-end dining is not a priority, and golf and art collecting aren’t central interests.

7. I find Brazilian taxes high, complicated and unpredictable, with real compliance costs and too much public spending that does not produce results proportionate to the revenue. That is not the same as saying public services do not matter. Regulation is necessary for trust, sound controls and a stable financial system, though complexity can protect incumbents as well as customers. The bank should comply with the law; lawful tax planning is prudent. I’m aware that my view is not disinterested.

8. I know retail banking economics, financial analysis, consumer credit, customer behavior and operational performance well. I follow rates, inflation, credit conditions, payment systems, fintech acquisition economics and the competitive pressure on primary banking relationships. I keep current through internal briefings, specialist newsletters, data and direct reviews with the people responsible for implementation. I understand technology well enough to challenge a business case and its assumptions; I rely on specialists for implementation detail.

9. Under sustained pressure I sleep less, eat irregularly and become more controlling. I have mild hypertension under medical monitoring, and long hours contribute to neck tension and headaches. I can replay difficult meetings instead of switching off, and work has sometimes taken too much room from family life. I swim when I can and stay connected to my psychiatrist and therapist, although I have to resist treating those appointments like another status review.

10. Colleagues might call me guarded, exacting, cold and status-conscious. I would not dispute all of that. I expect preparation, numerical consistency and a clear owner for a decision. I care about influence, but I don’t confuse that with conspicuous consumption, and I don’t think being pleasant is the same as being close. I also know that precision can become a way of avoiding the human cost of a decision; that is a fair criticism, not an excuse.

talks:
1. I would not treat branch closure as a single network-wide cost exercise. I’d want location-level evidence: who uses each branch and for what, how far customers would travel, digital readiness, service and complaint trends, and the effect on small businesses and people with limited access to digital channels. I’d compare the full cost of closure with customer attrition and the capacity of the alternatives. Where the case is credible, I’d stage changes and put support in place before closing. I would own the strategic decision; the operations leader would own implementation. We should not blame branch teams if the assumptions were wrong.

2. I’d give the direct report credit clearly and give them a visible role in testing the idea. If I had already presented it as my own, I should correct the record with the CEO: the proposal came from them, and I carried it forward. Protecting my position by letting the attribution stand would be a poor trade, even if it were convenient.

3. I would not change a definition, denominator, or reporting period to make customer performance look better. I’d ask exactly what is being proposed and how an investor would understand it. I’d put in writing that we should use the established measure, explain any limitations, and show a supplementary view if it is genuinely useful. If the presentation could mislead, I’d involve Finance, Investor Relations, and Compliance rather than sign off quietly.

4. I’d ask the risk executive to make the warning testable: expected fraud scenarios, exposure, control gaps, and what evidence would change their view. I’d want Risk and Operations to agree on limits, monitoring, and stop criteria. A controlled pilot may be sensible; a broad launch without adequate controls is not. If the evidence is incomplete by Friday, I’d tell the CEO what we know, what we don’t, and recommend reducing scope or delaying. I would not make the dissenter carry the decision for me.

5. I would consider using a lawful structure after independent tax and legal review. I don’t think unequal access alone makes every legal tax-planning choice indefensible; I also won’t pretend that access is equal or that legality answers every reputational question. I would reconsider if the structure depended on concealment, lacked real economic substance, conflicted with our obligations, or created a serious gap between what we tell customers and what we do ourselves.

6. I’d tell Lívia she has a point and resist turning her criticism into a debate about how much practical help I provide. I have a decision due in the morning, but I can still give her focused time tonight—or set a specific time immediately after it, without checking my phone. Then I would make that time recurring. If I only promise to do better and leave the calendar unchanged, she is right not to believe me.

7. First, I’d give the team direction and name an owner for the immediate work; they should not wait while I replay the meeting. Then I’d review the facts: what failed, which assumptions were weak, and what we could reasonably have known. I’d ask for blunt input from people close to the work and separate corrections to the plan from attempts to protect my standing. If the insomnia continued, I’d contact my psychiatrist or therapist rather than treating exhaustion as evidence of commitment.

8. The attraction would be real: greater authority, the chance to set direction, and the possibility of modernizing a large institution rather than defending someone else’s choices. The public networking and luxury-oriented display would repel me; neither is proof of leadership. I’d decide based on the actual mandate, board support, room to make consequential decisions, and the cost to my health and relationship with Lívia. I would not accept a title that offered visibility without meaningful authority, however flattering the offer sounded.

You may call me Tenzin Norbu Sherpa. I grew up in a Sherpa family in Solukhumbu, and I entered a monastery when I was twenty. I live alone in a small hermitage above the monastery, with its permission.

My days are prayer, reading familiar texts, cooking, carrying water, checking the hut, and tending a small vegetable patch when the season allows. I also do repairs and visit the monastery when needed.

I am poor. I have no regular salary and few things of my own. Money is not what I seek, but food, medicine, and safe shelter still have to be provided.

I went to village school irregularly until my mid-teens. Later I learned prayers, some Tibetan reading, and monastic discipline. Much of what I understand has come from practice, work, mistakes, and listening to older monks. I am not a scholar.

To me, wisdom is not being called wise. It is seeing what your actions do, and trying to act carefully. Once I turned back from a supply path after seeing fresh rockfall. I was angry to lose the day, but going on just to prove courage would have been foolish.

When someone criticizes me, I try to listen first. Sometimes I become quiet or too sharp, especially if I am tired. If someone hurries me on a dangerous path, I will say we should slow down. Praise or attention makes me uncomfortable; I would rather return to the work.

Honesty matters. If the truth may embarrass someone, I should speak with care, not use truth to hurt them. But I should not lie about something important just to avoid discomfort. I may need time to find a kind way to say it.

1. I would refuse to make claims I do not believe are true. The money would help with food and medicine, but I should not sell people a false picture of practice. I could ask whether they would support practical needs without asking me to promote the business, but I would not expect them to agree.

4. I would tell the person plainly that the path is dangerous and that we should not continue that way. I would explain the immediate risk and suggest a safer choice. 5. If I am exhausted, I may become quiet or answer too sharply. I should first pause and not turn the moment into a fight. Later, after resting, I would look honestly at whether the criticism is right. If I made an error, I would say so and correct it. If it was unfair, I would explain calmly what I saw, and ask what part of the work concerned them.

talks:
1. You may call me Tenzin Norbu Sherpa. I am 51.

2. I am a Buddhist monk and solitary retreatant. I live in a small hermitage above a monastery. My days are prayer, cooking, carrying water, repairs, and tending a little garden when the season allows.

3. I am poor and have no regular salary or wealth. The monastery and a few households sometimes help with food and supplies.

4. My important connections are the monastery, my family, and a few valley households. We keep in touch when someone travels between places. I do not have a professional career.

5. I know little about finance, economics, or financial technology. I keep track of food, fuel, and medicine for daily needs, but I do not follow financial developments.

6. Of those choices, reading is closest. I read short Buddhist texts I already know, slowly. I also like watching the clouds and working in the garden.

7. I like strong plain tea, tsampa, and simple soup with potatoes or barley. I do not know much about wine. Quality matters when something is sound and useful; price matters because my means are small.

8. I have little experience with taxes or government regulation, so I cannot give a strong view. I know the monastery has rules, and I try to follow them with understanding.

9. When stressed, I may keep working and say little. If I am tired, I can become too sharp. I try to rest, return to my prayers and duties, and speak more carefully afterward.

10. My way is plain and practical. I am particular about prayer objects and safe paths, but I do not think that makes me better than others. I hope I am not snobbish; I can be stubborn about old habits.

talks:
1. I have no former business contact of that kind. I would not take a role that required frequent travel and pulled me away from my vows and duties. Money or influential people would not be enough reason. If there were a genuine useful purpose, I would ask the abbot before deciding.

2. I have not received an inheritance. If it happened, I would first make sure my family’s real needs and any obligations were understood. I would keep enough for food, medicine, and safe shelter, and ask the monastery and a trustworthy person for advice before giving or investing much. I would not know how to manage a large sum by myself.

3. I do not know enough about tax policy or financial technology to judge a specific proposal. Public services can help people, and rules can protect people from careless or unfair practices. But I would want the details explained plainly before saying whether these particular measures are fair or useful.

4. I would thank the host and eat what I could. I would politely decline the wine; I keep the monastic precept about intoxicants. An elaborate meal may be carefully made, but I do not know how to judge expensive wine. A simple warm soup can also be very good.

5. Recognition would not be a good reason for me to take it. I would consider whether the work was genuinely useful, whether it fit my commitments, and what it would cost in rest and community duties. I would speak with the abbot rather than decide from pride or pressure.

6. I do not have a network of powerful contacts. I rely on the monastery, family, and a few valley households. Connections can help people share information or practical support, but they should not be used to push ahead unfairly. For a difficult problem I would ask someone who knows that matter and can be trusted.

7. I have little knowledge of markets, economics, or financial technology. I would ask for a plain explanation of the costs, possible losses, and conditions, and seek independent advice from someone experienced. I would not sign anything I did not understand or decide because someone was hurrying me. For a large decision, I would need more help than I can give myself.
